newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia cabinet denies plan to legalise Romanovs.
newsitem.headline: Russia cabinet denies plan to legalise Romanovs.

text.p: The Russian government has rejected the idea of granting official status to the Romanov family which ruled the country as an all-powerful dynasty between 1613 and 1917, Interfax news agency said on Sunday.
It quoted the office of the First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov as saying that about two months ago such project had circulated in the cabinet.
"But the project was rejected at a very initial stage and there was absolutely no follow-up on it," Interfax quoted an aide to Nemtsov as saying.
"As of now there are no documents or projects on this problem in the government," the unnamed aide said.

Russian media have given wide space to rumours that President Boris Yeltsin or his government might grant some official status to the exiled descendants of the Romanovs whose last tsar, Nicolas II, was murdered with his family by the Bolsheviks in 1918.

Yeltsin's spokesman earlier denied the Kremlin was considering any such step but the family insist it has had talks on being granted a special status to allow the 16-year-old Grand Prince Georgy to live in Russia and attend a naval college once he finishes school.
The rumours have also been fuelled by plans to swear in Georgy as head of the imperial house at a private ceremony in Russia.

Officials from the Russian Nobility Assembly, whose members claim descent from the tsarist ruling class, told reporters late last month the oath-taking ceremony may be held on June 21 in Kostroma, an ancient city 350 km (200 miles) north of Moscow.
But they added it might be delayed for a week or more because Georgy's exam schedule at his school in Madrid was not quite certain.

The members of the Assembly have played down the political significance of Georgy's solemn pledge, part of a coming-of-age ceremony following his 16th birthday last March, to uphold the values of the Russian Orthodox Church and serve his country.
